lessons.title: Pre-Money, Post-Money and Price Per Share

children.text: A term sheet lands in your inbox: "Investment of ₹3 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹12 crore." Quick, what percentage does the investor get? If you said 25%, you have just made the most common mistake in startup investing. The answer is 20%. This lesson gives you the three numbers behind every priced round, pre-money, post-money and price per share, and shows why one word in a term sheet can move lakhs of rupees between founders and investors.

body.text: Pre-money is what the company is worth before the new cheque. Post-money is pre-money plus the cheque. An investor's ownership is always the cheque divided by post-money, never by pre-money.

children.text: The Four Formulas You Need
Every priced round in India, from a ₹25 lakh angel round to a ₹500 crore Series D, runs on the same four relationships.

body.caption: 1. The cheque is added to the company
2. Ownership is measured against the bigger, post-money number

body.latex: \text{Price per share} = \frac{\text{Pre-money valuation}}{\text{Fully diluted shares before the round}}
body.caption: 3. The price is set by the existing share count
4. The cheque buys shares at that price

children.text: The term
pre-money valuation
describes the company as it stands. The
post-money valuation
describes it after the new money has arrived, and that money is now part of what the company owns.

markDefs.definition: The agreed value of a company immediately before a new investment, based on its fully diluted shares before the round.
The value of a company immediately after a new investment: pre-money valuation plus the new money.

children.text: Worked Example: Rangrez Raises ₹3 Crore

Rangrez Textiles Private Limited is a fictional Jaipur brand selling hand-block-printed clothing online. Before its seed round it has 1,20,000 fully diluted shares: co-founder Aditi holds 60,000, co-founder Kabir holds 40,000, and an ESOP pool holds 20,000. A seed fund agrees to invest ₹3 crore at a pre-money valuation of ₹12 crore.

Check it the other way. After the round there are 1,20,000 + 30,000 = 1,50,000 shares. At ₹1,000 each, that is ₹15 crore, matching the post-money valuation. The fund owns 30,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 20%, which is also ₹3 crore ÷ ₹15 crore. When the share count method and the valuation method give the same answer, your maths is right.

body.caption: Rangrez cap table before and after the seed round (fully diluted)

body.title: Rangrez ownership after the seed round (%)

body.text: Every existing holder was diluted by the same proportion. Aditi went from 50% to 40%, Kabir from 33.33% to 26.67% and the ESOP pool from 16.67% to 13.33%. Each kept exactly 80% of their previous stake, because the new investor took 20% of the post-money company.

body.title: An angel's stake
body.prompt: An angel invests ₹50 lakh in a startup at a pre-money valuation of ₹4.5 crore. What percentage of the company does the angel own after the round?
body.explanation: Post-money = ₹4.5 crore + ₹0.5 crore = ₹5 crore. Ownership = ₹50 lakh ÷ ₹5 crore = 10%. Dividing by the pre-money figure instead would give 11.1%, which overstates the stake.

children.text: One Word, Very Different Deals
Now suppose the term sheet had said "₹3 crore at a post-money valuation of ₹12 crore". The headline number is the same, but the deal is not.

body.caption: "₹12 crore pre-money" vs "₹12 crore post-money" for the same ₹3 crore cheque

body.title: Ownership after the round under each reading (%)

children.text: Same cheque, same headline number, and the fund walks away with a quarter of the company instead of a fifth. For the founders, the post-money reading means selling each share for ₹750 instead of ₹1,000, a 25% lower price.

body.text: Never accept "valued at ₹X crore" without asking "pre-money or post-money, and on a fully diluted basis?" Founders tend to quote the bigger number, and investors tend to prefer the reading that gives them more ownership. Get it in writing before you calculate anything.

body.label: Shark Tank India shorthand
body.context: When a founder on Shark Tank India asks for a sum "for X% equity", the implied valuation includes the sharks' own money. It is a post-money figure. The pre-money value of the business is ₹25 crore minus ₹50 lakh, or ₹24.5 crore.

body.title: Read the ask
body.question: A founder asks for ₹1 crore for 4% equity. What pre-money valuation does that imply?
body.explanation: ₹1 crore ÷ 4% = ₹25 crore post-money. Subtract the ₹1 crore investment and the pre-money valuation is ₹24 crore.

children.text: Why Price Per Share Is the Number to Track

Valuations make headlines, but price per share is what you actually pay, and it is the cleanest way to compare rounds. Every investor in the same round, from the lead fund to a ₹5 lakh angel, should pay the same price per share for the same instrument.

body.title: Why the price uses fully diluted shares

children.text: Suppose Rangrez's founders argued that the ₹12 crore pre-money should be divided only by the 1,00,000 issued founder shares, ignoring the 20,000-share ESOP pool.
Price per share: ₹12 crore ÷ 1,00,000 = ₹1,200
New shares for ₹3 crore: ₹3 crore ÷ ₹1,200 = 25,000
Fully diluted shares after: 1,00,000 + 20,000 + 25,000 = 1,45,000
Seed fund's real stake: 25,000 ÷ 1,45,000 = 17.24%
The fund pays ₹3 crore expecting 20% and receives 17.24% once the ESOP pool is counted. This is why term sheets define the price on a fully diluted pre-money share count, and why you should too.
When Rangrez raises its Series A, you compare the new price per share with ₹1,000. A higher price is an up round, a lower one is a down round, and the ratio between them is the step-up.

body.latex: \text{Step-up multiple} = \frac{\text{New round price per share}}{\text{Previous round price per share}}
body.caption: Above 1 is an up round, below 1 is a down round

body.title: Series A price
body.prompt: Two years later, Rangrez raises a Series A at a pre-money valuation of ₹45 crore. It still has 1,50,000 fully diluted shares before this round. What is the Series A price per share, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹45 crore ÷ 1,50,000 = ₹3,000 per share. That is a 3x step-up from the ₹1,000 seed price. The seed fund's 30,000 shares are now worth 30,000 × ₹3,000 = ₹9 crore on paper, three times its ₹3 crore investment.

body.title: The core identity
body.textWithBlank: Post-money valuation equals pre-money valuation plus the new ___.
body.explanation: The new cash becomes an asset of the company, so the company is worth that much more immediately after the round.

body.title: "Raising ₹2 crore at ₹10 crore"
body.scenario: A Kochi healthtech founder tells a room of angels at a pitch event: "We are raising ₹2 crore at a ₹10 crore valuation. Minimum cheque ₹10 lakh." The deck has no cap table.
body.prompt: What stake would a ₹10 lakh cheque buy under each possible reading, and what would you ask before committing?
body.modelAnswer:
If ₹10 crore is pre-money: post-money is ₹12 crore. The whole round buys 16.67%, and a ₹10 lakh cheque buys ₹10 lakh ÷ ₹12 crore = 0.83%.

If ₹10 crore is post-money: pre-money is ₹8 crore. The whole round buys 20%, and a ₹10 lakh cheque buys ₹10 lakh ÷ ₹10 crore = 1.00%.

Questions to ask:
1. Is ₹10 crore pre-money or post-money?
2. How many fully diluted shares exist before the round, including the ESOP pool, and what is the price per share?
3. Are there convertible notes or iSAFEs that will convert in this round and add shares?
4. Is the ESOP pool being increased as part of this round, and is that increase inside the pre-money?
5. Can I see the pre-round and post-round cap table on a fully diluted basis?

cards.definition: The agreed value of the company immediately before new money comes in.
Pre-money valuation plus the new investment.
New investment divided by post-money valuation.
Pre-money valuation divided by fully diluted shares before the round.
The new round's price per share divided by the previous round's price per share.
A round priced higher per share than the previous round.
A round priced lower per share than the previous round.

points: Post-money valuation = pre-money valuation + new investment.
Ownership is the investment divided by post-money, never by pre-money.
Price per share = pre-money valuation ÷ fully diluted shares before the round. New shares = investment ÷ price.
The same headline valuation read as pre-money or post-money can shift ownership by several percentage points.
"₹X for Y% equity" implies a post-money valuation of X ÷ Y.
Compare rounds by price per share. The step-up multiple tells you whether a round is up or down.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Rangrez Textiles and the other startups mentioned are fictional. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid and can result in the loss of your entire capital. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
